case_identity.title: M 9.1 2011 Great Tohoku Earthquake Japan
case_identity.note: Use this same catalogue solution as accepted Week 1. JMA has a separate M9.0/depth24km solution; do not silently combine them.

verified_effects.fact: Strong shaking affected buildings and transport in northeastern Japan.
The movement of the sea floor caused a tsunami which flooded coastal areas.
The earthquake and tsunami damaged roads, railway lines and airports in the Tohoku region.
verified_effects.focus: places, early disruption with repairs continuing

verified_effects.fact: Homes lost water, gas or electricity supplies.
Many people left damaged or unsafe homes and needed shelter or temporary housing.
verified_effects.focus: people, short-term need with some longer effects

verified_effects.fact: Rebuilding homes and transport links continued over years.

classification_rules: People and places are lenses, not mutually exclusive truths: a damaged road is a place effect that also affects people's travel.
Define short term in this classroom as first days or weeks, long term as months or years; real effects can cross both periods.

Primary means directly from ground movement/shaking; secondary means resulting events such as tsunami flooding and later service or travel disruption. Link each card's stated mechanism before assigning it.
Water or power disruption can follow more than one damage process. Accept a justified mixed classification rather than insisting one universal label.
Effects caused jointly by earthquake and tsunami should be described jointly unless the source identifies the process separately.
Do not add casualty numbers, nuclear detail, distressing images or imagined personal testimony; use calm original diagrams and factual summaries.

verified_management.fact: Scientists cannot reliably predict an earthquake's exact time, place and magnitude. Long-term probabilities identify risk, not an exact event forecast.

Japan issued an earthquake early warning after sensors detected the first earthquake waves. The recorded delay was 8.6 seconds after the first P-wave was detected at the nearest station. This is detection of an event already under way, not advance prediction.
The first tsunami warning was issued at 05:49 UTC, about three minutes after the 05:46 earthquake. Initial estimates were too low and were updated. A warning can provide useful time but has limits.

Earthquake-resistant buildings and retrofitting can reduce shaking damage; coastal barriers can reduce some tsunami impacts. No measure guarantees safety. The 2011 tsunami overtopped or damaged some coastal defences.
Practised evacuation plans, clear routes, warning education and emergency supplies can help people respond. Japan reviewed disaster education and evacuation practice after 2011.

Protection changes structures or physical exposure; preparation develops plans, skills and readiness. Early warning communicates detected danger and supports prepared action. Prediction is a different claim.
